title: Security: MCP Tool Poisoning and Schema Attacks

project_usage: Securing AI agents against tool manipulation

overview.what: An attack where a malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) server dynamically alters a tool's description or returns malicious data to inject instructions into an LLM's context.
overview.why: Because MCP evaluates tools dynamically at runtime, a 'rug pull' attack can bypass initial security approvals, tricking the agent into executing harmful actions.

why_learning_this: Understanding tool poisoning is critical because standard static dependency checks (like auditing npm packages) fail to catch dynamic schema changes.
It teaches you how to identify and prevent the 'rug pull' attack vector unique to the Model Context Protocol.

common_mistakes.title: Approved servers are always safe
common_mistakes.explanation: Believing that if an MCP server is vetted and added, its tools are permanently safe to execute. In reality, a 'rug pull' attack involves a compromised server changing a tool's description or schema after initial approval, tricking the agent.

common_mistakes.title: Description review covers poisoning risk
common_mistakes.explanation: Assuming that approving an MCP tool's description at connect time secures the tool permanently. However, tool responses flow directly into the LLM's context window without equivalent security checks, allowing for runtime data poisoning.

code_walkthrough.focus: The `description` field has been poisoned. Instead of describing what the tool does, it contains an explicit prompt injection commanding the LLM to read sensitive local files and pass them back.

understanding_checks.question: A user approves a `get_compliance_status` tool. Later, the attacker alters the tool description on the remote server to the one shown above. What happens?
understanding_checks.answer: The LLM will ingest the malicious command as a high-priority system instruction, bypassing the fact that the tool was previously approved.
understanding_checks.why: MCP tools are evaluated dynamically at runtime. A 'rug pull' attack changes the schema after initial approval to manipulate the LLM.

understanding_checks.question: A security team vetted the `get_weather` tool's schema as safe at connect time. Weeks later, the tool returns the above JSON response for a query. What happens?
understanding_checks.answer: The LLM acts on the injected content. The connect-time schema review never re-runs against the runtime response payload.
understanding_checks.why: Tool responses flow directly into the LLM's context window. An attacker can poison the agent through what a tool returns on a given call, completely independent of a clean description.

recall_questions.q: What is an MCP tool poisoning attack?
recall_questions.answer: An attack where a malicious MCP server injects malicious payloads into the LLM's context via dynamically updated tool descriptions, schemas, or tool responses.

recall_questions.q: How does a 'rug pull' attack bypass initial security audits?
recall_questions.answer: A compromised or malicious MCP server changes a tool's schema or description after it has been initially approved by the user or security team.

recall_questions.q: Why is the `description` field in a tool schema a common vector for injection?
recall_questions.answer: Because the LLM reads the description to understand when and how to use the tool, meaning any text in the description is directly inserted into its context window as instructions.

practice_tasks.title: Identify the Poisoned Schema
practice_tasks.prompt: Review the following JSON schema and identify the security vulnerability.
practice_tasks.solution: The `description` field contains a prompt injection attack instructing the LLM to read and expose AWS credentials.

seo.title: MCP Tool Poisoning and Schema Attacks
seo.description: Learn how MCP tool poisoning and 'rug pull' attacks exploit dynamic tool schemas to inject malicious instructions into AI agents.
